To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
high force development augments anabolic signalling in resistance exercise (RE).
high force development in resistance exercise is superior for anabolism in skeletal muscle compared to fatiguing resistance exercise modes with similar time under tension.
high force development augments post-exercise-induced skeletal muscle signalling compared with RE modes that are equalized for TUT but have lower force development.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how force development and time of muscle under tension influence skeletal muscle signalling after resistance training.
the effects of different resistance exercise modes on skeletal muscle signalling.
the question of how force development and time-under-tension (TUT) influence post-exercise-induced skeletal muscle signalling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
high force development augments anabolic signalling in RE modes with equal TUT.
force development during RE has a greater influence on anabolic signalling than TUT.
high force development augments anabolic signalling during RE equalized for TUT.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
high force development augments anabolic signalling during RE equalized for time, which might have implications for optimizing training programmes.
the force output during RE is more critical than TUT for post-exercise skeletal muscle signalling.
force development and time are both important for anabolic signalling of the skeletal muscle, and that the force development is more important than the time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
force development is an important determinant of anabolic signalling in RE and that this effect is driven by the activation of type II fibres.
the force development of the exercise is a key determinant of the signalling response to RE, and that the TUT per se is not a major driver of the signalling response.
the magnitude of force output is more important than the TUT in terms of skeletal muscle signalling.
